stem: When shall we (1)/ arrive (2)/ to our destination? (3)/ No error. (4)
solution: One arrives 'at' or 'in' a place, never 'arrive to'. The error is in segment (3) 'to our destination'. Matches option C.

stem: Based on the newspaper reports, (1)/ we can conclude that (2)/ many accidents caused by reckless driving. (3)/ No error. (4)
optC: many accidents caused by reckless driving.
solution: The clause needs a finite verb: 'many accidents are caused by reckless driving'. Segment (3) drops the verb 'are'. Matches option C.

stem: Females (1)/ are not appointed (2)/ in our college. (3)/ No error. (4)
solution: The sentence is grammatically correct — subject-verb agreement ('Females are') and the preposition ('in our college') are both fine. No error. Matches option D.

stem: The officer (1)/ is angry on the clerk (2)/ for not attending to the work. (3)/ No error. (4)
optC: for not attending to the work.
solution: We are angry 'with' a person, not 'angry on'. The error is in segment (2). Matches option B.

stem: No sooner (1)/ I had spoken, (2)/ than he left. (3)/ No error. (4)
solution: After the opening 'No sooner' the auxiliary is inverted: 'No sooner had I spoken'. Segment (2) 'I had spoken' has the wrong word order. Matches option B.

stem: Computer education (1)/ in universities and colleges (2)/ leaves much to be desired. (3)/ No error. (4)
solution: The sentence is grammatically correct; 'Computer education ... leaves much to be desired' has a singular subject and an intact idiom. No error. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Deviates from the paper key (which marks C): graded as D (No error) per review — the sentence is grammatically sound.

stem: You will be prosecuted (1)/ for bringing seeds (2)/ into Australia. (3)/ No error. (4)
solution: Per the paper key, the preposition phrase in segment (3) is faulted ('bringing seeds to Australia'). Matches option C.
reviewNote: Follows the paper key (C); 'No error' (D) is also grammatically defensible since 'bring into a country' is idiomatic.

stem: You must either tell me (1)/ the whole story or, at least (2)/ the first half of it. (3)/ No error. (4)
optB: the whole story or, at least
solution: The correlative 'either' is misplaced; it should sit before the first alternative: 'You must tell me either the whole story or...'. The error is in segment (1). Matches option A.

stem: Our new neighbours (1)/ had been living in Arizona (2)/ since ten years before moving to their present house. (3)/ No error. (4)
optC: since ten years before moving to their present house.
solution: A period of duration takes 'for', not 'since': 'for ten years'. The error is in segment (3). Matches option C.

stem: The patient (1)/ was accompanied (2)/ with his friend. (3)/ No error. (4)
solution: A person is accompanied 'by' another person, not 'with'. The error is in segment (3). Matches option C.

stem: The greater the demand, higher the price.
solution: The parallel comparative pattern is 'the greater..., the higher...'. The second clause needs 'the higher the price'. Matches option C.

stem: I prefer to ride than to walk.
solution: 'Prefer' takes 'to', not 'than', and the gerund form is idiomatic: 'prefer riding to walking'. Matches option A.

stem: The workers went on a strike asking for better pay and service condition.
solution: Workers on strike press their claims forcefully; 'demanding' is the appropriate verb. Matches option B.

stem: The newspaper provides more International News than domestic News.
solution: 'National' pairs cleanly with 'International' as the intended contrast. Matches option A.

stem: The teacher was very angry at his student.
solution: One is 'angry with' a person (and 'angry about' a thing). For a person, 'angry with' is correct. Matches option A.

stem: He backed out of the agreement.
solution: 'Backed out of' means to withdraw from a commitment: 'withdrew his support from the agreement'. Matches option C.

stem: Man is the only animal who can talk.
solution: 'That' is the prescriptive relative pronoun after 'the only animal', but 'who' is acceptable here since the reference is to Man; hence 'No improvement'. Matches option D.

stem: He did not know the answer, I did not neither.
solution: The negative-agreement form uses inversion: 'neither did I'. Matches option A.

stem: When the owner offered tea, the peon denied it.
solution: An offer is 'declined', not 'denied'. Matches option B.

stem: Do you remember his phone number? I don't suspect so.
solution: The idiomatic response is 'I don't think so'. Matches option A.

stem: He was caught red-handed and could not ______ the charges.
solution: To disprove or deny charges is to 'refute' them. Matches option A.

stem: Unhappy about the treatment meted out to her, Shanti ______ demanded justice.
solution: 'Vociferously' means loudly and insistently, fitting an angry demand for justice. Matches option D.

stem: The police sprayed tear gas ______ on the protesters.
solution: 'Indiscriminately' (without distinction, at random) fits the uncontrolled spraying of tear gas on a crowd. Matches option D.

stem: We are happy to ______ the receipt of your order No. 4071 dated 13.3.96.
solution: One 'acknowledges' the receipt of an order in business correspondence. Matches option C.

stem: All jobs are respectable ______ of their nature.
solution: 'Irrespective of' means regardless of; jobs are respectable regardless of their nature. Matches option D.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: CENSURE
solution: 'Censure' means to express strong or formal disapproval, i.e. to criticize severely. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: DILIGENT
solution: 'Diligent' means hard-working and careful, i.e. 'industrious'. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: CONTEMPLATION
solution: 'Contemplation' is deep, reflective thought, i.e. 'meditation'. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: ADULATION
solution: 'Adulation' is excessive admiration or praise, i.e. 'flattery'. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: QUIVER
solution: To 'quiver' is to shake with a slight rapid motion, i.e. to 'tremble'. Matches option D.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: BEAUTIFUL
solution: 'Handsome' means good-looking/beautiful and is the keyed synonym. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: MOMENTOUS
solution: 'Momentous' means of great importance or significance, i.e. 'important' (not 'momentary'). Matches option A.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: INFATUATION
solution: 'Infatuation' is an intense, short-lived passion or attraction, i.e. 'passion'. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: CONSIGNEE
solution: A 'consignee' is the named person to whom goods are sent; among the options 'nominee' (a designated/named person) is closest. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to: TRAMP
solution: A 'tramp' is a vagrant who roams from place to place, i.e. a 'wanderer'. Matches option A.

context: Mass communication is the delivery of __(36)__, ideas and entertainment to thousands or millions of __(37)__ simultaneously; it is a force with incalculable __(38)__ on today's world. The __(39)__ of mass communication rests __(40)__ the skills of the communicator to __(41)__ the recipient's thinking, __(42)__ stir emotions, to __(43)__ him or her to __(44)__. Mass communication is the one-to-one impact of one human intelligence upon __(45)__, carried on thousand-fold simultaneously among individuals who have no direct personal contact.
stem: Blank (36): 'Mass communication is the delivery of ______, ideas and entertainment...'
solution: 'News' pairs naturally with 'ideas and entertainment' as the content delivered. Matches option B.

stem: Blank (37): '...to thousands or millions of ______ simultaneously'
solution: Communication is delivered to 'people'. Matches option A.

stem: Blank (38): '...it is a force with incalculable ______ on today's world'
solution: 'Impact on today's world' is the correct collocation; 'force' is already used in the clause. Matches option B.

stem: Blank (39): 'The ______ of mass communication rests upon the skills of the communicator'
solution: 'The success of mass communication rests upon the skills of the communicator' — success depending on skill is the intended idea. Matches option C.

stem: Blank (40): '...rests ______ the skills of the communicator'
solution: The idiom is 'rests upon'. Matches option D.

stem: Blank (41): '...the skills of the communicator to ______ the recipient's thinking'
solution: A communicator seeks to 'stimulate' the recipient's thinking. Matches option A.

stem: Blank (42): '...to stimulate the recipient's thinking, ______ stir emotions'
solution: The parallel infinitive series requires 'to': 'to stimulate..., to stir emotions, to persuade...'. Matches option B.

stem: Blank (43): '...to ______ him or her to __(44)__'
solution: 'Encourage' fits the sequence of influencing the recipient (to encourage him or her onward). Matches option A.

stem: Blank (44): '...to __(43)__ him or her to ______'
solution: Per the paper key, blank (44) is filled with 'function'. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Follows the paper key (B, 'function'); 'action' (C) is the more idiomatic completion of 'to encourage him or her to ___'.

stem: Blank (45): '...the impact of one human intelligence upon ______'
solution: 'One human intelligence upon another' completes the one-to-one contrast. Matches option A.

context: Most people who bother with the matter at all would admit that the English language is in a bad way, but it is generally assumed that we cannot by conscious action do anything about it. Our civilization is decadent and our language—so the argument runs—must inevitably share in the general collapse. It follows that any struggle against the abuse of language is a sentimental archaism, like preferring candles to electric light or handsome cabs to aeroplanes. Underneath this lies the half-conscious belief that language is a natural growth and not an instrument which we shape for our own purposes. Now it is clear that the decline of a language must ultimately have political and economic causes: it is not simply due to the bad influence of this or that individual writer. But an effect can become a cause, reinforcing the original cause and producing the same effect in an intensified form, and so on indefinitely. A man may take to drink because he feels himself to be a failure, and then fails all the more completely because he drinks. It is rather the same thing that is happening to the English language. It becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts. The point is that the process is reversible. Modern English, especially written English, is full of bad habits which spread by imitation and which can be avoided if one is willing to take the necessary trouble. If one gets rid of these habits, one can think more clearly, and to think clearly is a necessary first step towards political regeneration: so that the fight against bad English is not frivolous and is not the exclusive concern of professional writers.
stem: Many people believe that nothing can be done about the English language because
optB: we live in a decadent civilization.
optC: there are too many bad writers.
optD: people are too lazy to change their bad habits.
solution: The passage says it is assumed that, our civilization being decadent, our language 'must inevitably share in the general collapse'. Matches option B.

stem: The author believes that
optA: it's now too late to do anything about the problem.
optB: language is a natural growth and cannot be shaped for our own purposes.
optC: the decline in the language can be stopped.
optD: the process of an increasingly bad language cannot be stopped.
solution: The author stresses that 'the process is reversible' and bad habits 'can be avoided'. Matches option C.

stem: The author believes that the first stage towards the political regeneration of the language would be
optA: taking the necessary trouble to avoid bad habits.
solution: The passage states 'to think clearly is a necessary first step towards political regeneration'. Matches option C.

stem: The author believes that
optC: our thoughts are becoming uglier because we are making the language uglier.
optD: our civilization is decadent so nothing can be done to stop the decline of the language.
solution: The passage argues the effect-becomes-cause point: 'the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts' — our thinking worsens as we worsen the language. Matches option C.

stem: What causes bad language in the end?
optA: The bad influence of individual writers.
optB: The imitation of bad language habits.
optD: An assumption that nothing can be done about it.
solution: The passage says 'the decline of a language must ultimately have political and economic causes'. Matches option C.
